entry.evidence: Our goal is to determine the age of the ice, understand its overall geologic history, and evaluate its potential use as a paleoclimate archive.

steps.action: States the problem: no ice-core climate archive extends beyond about 0.8 Ma, and ancient near-surface ice under debris is contested.
steps.quote: we currently lack archives of climate information that extend beyond ∼ 0.8 Ma.

steps.action: Takes the prior surface-debris exposure age of the Ong Valley Middle ice (>1.1 Ma, likely >1.8 Ma) from Bibby et al. (2016).
steps.quote: Cosmogenic nuclide measurements from the supraglacial debris suggest an age of > 1.1 Ma but most likely > 1.8 Ma

steps.action: Sets the aim of dating the buried ice, reconstructing its geologic history, and judging its value as a paleoclimate archive.
steps.quote: Our goal is to determine the age of the ice

steps.action: Adopts as the working hypothesis that the Middle ice was emplaced in a single glacial advance with well-mixed inheritance.
steps.quote: we start with the simplest assumption that the deposit of the Middle ice is from a single glacial advance

steps.action: Places the pit and core at a central high point of the Middle drift, away from valley-wall input and where ice deformation should be least.
steps.quote: We chose this site because any deformation of the buried ice should be minimized at this location

steps.action: Digs a 62 cm pit, drills a 944 cm debris-rich ice core, samples erratic boulders, and describes the core as banded basal ice.
steps.quote: consistent with characteristics of basal ice expected during an advance of the Argosy Glacier

steps.action: Checks the 21Ne measurements against the CRONUS-A intercomparison standard and corrects 10Be and 26Al for procedural blanks run in each batch.
steps.quote: indistinguishable from the accepted value of 320 × 10 6 atoms g - 1

steps.action: Builds a numerical forward model of nuclide accumulation with depth in sublimating debris-rich ice under eroding till, including shielding mass, depth histories, and spallation plus muon production; fitted by fmincon with a 10 000-iteration Monte Carlo.
steps.quote: we apply a forward model which attempts to account for the geological processes

steps.action: Measures 10Be, 21Ne and 26Al in pit and core samples and 10Be and 21Ne in boulders; finds large downcore variation, including anomalously high and downcore-increasing concentrations.
steps.quote: exhibit anomalously high nuclide concentrations between 132 and 207 cm below the surface

steps.action: Derives that a single exposure history with constant inheritance requires concentrations to decrease monotonically with depth.
steps.quote: the concentration for a given cosmogenic nuclide in the englacial debris must decrease monotonically with depth

steps.action: Compares the expectation with the profile; several core sections increase with depth, so the single-exposure, constant-inheritance assumption fails for them.
steps.quote: are therefore not compatible with a single exposure history described above

steps.action: Revises the constant-inheritance auxiliary and splits the core into low-inheritance englacial units (S1, E1, E2) and recycled paleo-surface units (S2, S3, S4) with prior exposure.
steps.quote: englacial debris in various sections of the core have variable exposure histories prior to entrainment in the ice

steps.action: Adds an unplanned burial-dating constraint: the model is fitted to S1, E1 and E2 only, and S2-S4 must not have negative burial ages, which bounds the emplacement age from above.
steps.quote: This constraint is incorporated into the model fitting during parameter optimization

steps.action: Fits the constrained forward model by Monte Carlo and obtains emplacement age 2.95 +0.18/-0.22 Ma, sublimation 22.86 m/Myr, erosion 0.206 m/Myr, and inherited concentrations.
steps.quote: provide an ice emplacement age of 2.95 + 0.18 / - 0.22 Ma for the Middle ice

steps.action: Compares predicted with measured profiles and paired-nuclide ratios; S1, E1 and E2 are explained, S2-S4 are distinct.
steps.quote: it is therefore evident that these units can be explained with the exposure model

steps.action: Recomputes a minimum-assumption bound (zero erosion, inheritance set to the core minimum), giving an absolute minimum age of 1.331 Ma.
steps.quote: This age is derived from the minimum possible number of assumptions about the geologic history of the samples.

steps.action: Subtracts the modeled post-emplacement inventory from S2-S4 and computes apparent burial ages from three nuclide pairs: S2 3.2-4.2 Ma, S3 and S4 4.3-7.6 Ma.
steps.quote: The paleo-surface S3 and S4 indicate longer periods of burial

steps.action: Compares the fitted sublimation and erosion rates with published cosmogenic estimates from Ong Valley and the Transantarctic Mountains and finds broad agreement.
steps.quote: These rates broadly agree with a sublimation rate of 22.86 m Myr - 1 as reported here in Ong Valley.

steps.action: Rejects the much higher sublimation rates from vapor-diffusion models, since they imply 300-1500 m of lowering, against about 68 m allowed by moraines.
steps.quote: are inconsistent with glacial moraine elevations and field observations in Ong Valley

steps.action: After a systematic misfit in the near-surface pit samples that parameter changes cannot fix, proposes partial vertical mixing of the till by polygon activity.
steps.quote: suggests that partial vertical mixing of the supraglacial debris may have occurred

steps.action: Checks the ice age against independent boulder 10Be/21Ne steady-erosion exposure ages; drift-surface boulders give 1.8-3.5 Ma, consistent with the model.
steps.quote: therefore agree with our modeled age of 2.96 Ma for the Middle drift ice

steps.action: Compares the minimum S2 burial age with the fitted Middle-ice age and finds them consistent; S2 was surface debris overridden at about 3 Ma.
steps.quote: the minimum burial age of 3.21 ± 0.20 Ma for S2 agrees with the age of the Middle ice

steps.action: Poses two rival configurations for S3 and S4: an older ice mass underlying the Middle ice in place, or older ice entrained and mixed in; leaves them unresolved.
steps.quote: Regardless, either is possible, and geochemical analysis of the ice could potentially help resolve this.

steps.action: Bounds the older ice mass at 3.3-7.6 Ma using S2 exposure plus burial and the maximum burial ages, and gives 4.3-5.1 Ma as most likely from 26Al/10Be.
steps.quote: a more likely age for this older deposit would be 4.3–5.1 Ma

steps.action: Relates both ages to Pliocene glaciations; the older ice possibly matches the early Pliocene glaciation, and the 2.95 Ma ice cannot be assigned to a single event.
steps.quote: possibly coincided with the early Pliocene global glaciation (ca. 4.9–4.8 Ma)

steps.action: Keeps two stacked ice masses: Middle ice at 2.95 Ma with stated rates, and an older lower ice mass at about 4.3-5.1 Ma.
steps.quote: We find the age of the Middle drift ice mass to be 2.95 Ma

steps.action: Referee 1 asked for a fuller physical description of the core stratigraphy, placed earlier; the authors agreed to expand it.
steps.quote: We agree that the physical description of the ice core should be expanded

steps.action: Referee 1 asked that core units be defined descriptively from stratigraphy rather than from nuclide data; the authors kept the nuclide-based units, saying sampling was not dictated by core characteristics.
steps.quote: it does not change our general approach to analyzing the core for three reasons

steps.action: Referee 1 asked that the downcore nuclide variation be described and quantified in the Results; the authors expanded the Results section.
steps.quote: We agree and will expand and add more details to the results section.

steps.action: Referee 1 suggested moving the bulk of the model description to the supplement; the authors kept it in the main text as the novel contribution.
steps.quote: we feel that it needs to be in the body of the paper rather than in an appendix

steps.action: In answer to the structure complaint, the authors agreed to state early that the paper starts from the single-advance assumption and adapts to the data (now §3 ¶5).
steps.quote: We can improve this by stating this explicitly early in the paper.

steps.action: The authors agreed to add an opening paragraph on shielding and production principles and to clarify how burial dating enters the model optimization versus the later burial-age calculation.
steps.quote: this section would benefit from the addition of a paragraph in the beginning which states the basic principles of shielding

steps.action: Referee 1 questioned the singular and plural 'ice mass' terminology; the authors kept 'ice masses' as reflecting the result of two advances.
steps.quote: Therefore, we need to refer to them as ice masses.

steps.action: The authors agreed to clarify that 'paleo-surface' does not imply an in situ surface (now in §6.1 ¶4).
steps.quote: In reference to the paleo surface, we do not imply that it is in situ. We will clarify this in the manuscript.

steps.action: Referee 2 asked why debris concentration is not a model input; the authors added an explanation (now §4.4 ¶1).
steps.quote: Yes, we will address this in the text

steps.action: Referee 2 asked them to specify that monotonic decrease is judged across the entire profile; the authors amended the text (now §6.1 ¶3).
steps.quote: We agree and will amend the text accordingly.

steps.action: Referee 2 asked for the Figure 7 uncertainty boxes and segment lines to be explained; the authors added this to the caption.
steps.quote: We will add the description of the horizontal/vertical boxes to the figure caption.

steps.action: Referee 2 queried the separately listed surface sample in the fitting set; the authors folded it into S1.
steps.quote: The surface sample is included in S1 and should not be listed individually.

steps.action: Referee 2 asked whether any samples were unused; the authors added that all non-fitted samples serve as burial constraints (now §6.2 ¶3).
steps.quote: Any samples not used for model fitting are used as burial constraints.

end.claim: The upper section of the Ong Valley ice core was emplaced 2.95 +0.18/-0.22 Ma (sublimation 22.86 m/Myr, erosion 0.206 m/Myr), and the lower section belongs to a separate, older ice mass estimated at 4.3-5.1 Ma.

decisive_move.sentence: Fitting the forward nuclide-accumulation model to the englacial units under the burial constraint from the recycled paleo-surface units yields the 2.95 Ma emplacement age and the inherited inventories from which the older-ice burial ages follow.

gates.evidence: Coring aimed to date the ice under a single-advance assumption, but sampling used all available mineral matter and was not hypothesis-directed (AC2 ¶4). The single-advance model could and did fail for part of the core (§6.1 ¶2), and the independent boulder ages could have disagreed (§7.5 ¶5). The S2 agreement is partly built in by the burial constraint (§6.2 ¶3). Burial dating was 'not originally planned for' (§3 ¶5), and no analysis plan was fixed in advance; only the Bibby-based initial guesses and the LGM exclusion threshold were set before fitting (§4.4.5 ¶2).

Accelerator mass spectrometry for 10Be/9Be and 26Al/27Al (LLNL-CAMS, PRIME)
Noble gas mass spectrometer ('Ohio' line, BGC) for 21Ne
Reduced chi-squared misfit and 10 000-iteration Monte Carlo uncertainty propagation
Constrained nonlinear optimization (MATLAB fmincon) and numerical integration

novelty_claims.quote: [...] novel dating application of cosmogenic nuclides which aims to quantify a complex exposure history of this buried ice mass.
These ancient ice masses represent new opportunities for gathering ancient climate information.
we show that exposure–burial dating of cosmogenic nuclides measured in situ in basal ice debris layers can be used for age constraint of past ice [...]

limits: Sub-claims sit at different statuses. The Middle-ice age and rates are estimate_with_resolution. The older ice mass at 4.3-5.1 Ma is best_explanation within bounds of 3.3-7.6 Ma, and whether it underlies the Middle ice in place or was entrained is unresolved (§7.6 ¶3). Partial vertical mixing of the till is a best_explanation of the pit misfit and is not tested (§7.4). The correlation with Pliocene glaciations is explicitly speculative (§7.7 ¶2). The units S1-S4 and E1-E2 are defined from the nuclide data themselves, not from stratigraphy; the referee's request to define them descriptively was declined. Production-rate uncertainties are excluded from the Monte Carlo, and constant sublimation is assumed. The S2 burial-age agreement is partly built in by the burial constraint. The paper says its order follows the actual course of the work (§3 ¶5; AC2 ¶11); the step order here is taken from that self-report and cannot be verified, so it is inference. Which review promises were implemented is inferred by matching the response letters to the published text; no tracked-changes version was supplied. The erosion rate (0.206) is lower than Bibby et al.'s 0.89 m/Myr but is presented as agreeing with the wider Dry Valleys range, not as a correction.

disagreements.target: Bibby et al. (2016) surface-debris exposure dating of the Middle drift (>1.1 Ma)
disagreements.support: The paper argues that surface exposure dating can give only a minimum age, and replaces it with a depth-profile forward model plus burial constraint that yields about 2.95 Ma.
disagreements.quote: a surficial exposure dating is expected to yield only a minimum age

disagreements.target: Sublimation rates from modeled water vapor diffusion (Hindmarsh et al., 1998; McKay et al., 1998; Kowalewski et al., 2006; Hagedorn et al., 2007; McKay, 2008; Schorghofer, 2009)
disagreements.support: Rates of 100-500 m/Myr would imply 300-1500 m of surface lowering, inconsistent with moraine elevations and the about 68 m inferred here.
disagreements.quote: [...] from modeled water vapor diffusion are orders of magnitude higher

disagreements.target: No vertical mixing in supraglacial debris (Bibby et al., 2016; Morgan et al., 2010a, b)
disagreements.support: A systematic model misfit for the near-surface pit samples, and paired ratios below the steady-erosion zone, are explained by partial mixing from active polygons.
disagreements.quote: It has previously been suggested that no vertical mixing occurs in the supraglacial debris layers in Ong valley

alternatives_considered.alternatives: Fit all samples with constant inheritance
alternatives_considered.reason: Constant inheritance can only fit monotonically decreasing samples

alternatives_considered.chosen: No nucleogenic 21Ne correction for model-fitted debris samples; correction applied for boulders and burial-dating samples
alternatives_considered.reason: Nucleogenic 21Ne is equivalent to inherited 21Ne in the model

alternatives_considered.chosen: Exclude production-rate uncertainty from the Monte Carlo
alternatives_considered.reason: All samples are from the same location and share one surface production rate

alternatives_considered.alternatives: Sublimation decreasing as the debris thickens (Mackay and Marchant, 2016)

alternatives_considered.chosen: Partial vertical mixing of the supraglacial debris
alternatives_considered.alternatives: Lower sublimation rate, higher erosion rate, or younger emplacement age
alternatives_considered.reason: The parameter changes do not improve the fit to the near-surface pit samples

alternatives_considered.chosen: Boulder ages from a steady-state erosion solution with paired 10Be/21Ne
alternatives_considered.reason: Discordant 10Be and 21Ne ages show the boulders have eroded

alternatives_considered.reason: It is unclear whether S3 and S4 are the same or different units

alternatives_considered.reason: No obvious stratigraphic boundary; steep disturbed fabric favors mixing
